title: Versatility, record-company pigeonholing and the Music Commission
summary: He can play everything from R&B to fusion, complains record companies want one mode, and talks of his Music Commission appointment and the workshop's aim of freedom for modern jazz players.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: Record labels, producers and the business of making albums

blocks.x: It just depends on the setting. I can play everything from the Little Richards to whatever is fusion to all of that. And I think to a large degree that that has been our problem. People having record companies sometimes want you to have, to market you, they want you to record in one mode. And you know I know personally I can sing, I can sing jazz, I can sing rock and roll, or whatever. And when you're promoting yourself no one wants to hear you blow your horn. And since I've come to that realization I sometimes suppress what my opinions, I mean be kind of careful about where I'll say them, you know, because of how it may be construed. But I certainly think that there's a much broader base and more people that deserve higher recognition. Not just because of what they're doing currently, but because of what they have contributed to the people who sometimes are given credit for being innovators of what's happening now. They've actually taken all of those things from these guys. And I think maybe someday we can come up with a list of people that I think that should be more recognized. I mean there are so many players that have become just frustrated with the way that they've been treated in this town. And you would think with the rise of tourism, I'm on the board of the Black Tourism Center, and I've just been appointed to the Music Commission in New Orleans. And one of the things that I want to push for is higher visibility of guys that'll be selected by people who know, not necessarily people who choose who's the most popular and the most easy to get along with. Because a lot of times a lot of the serious players are shoved in the corner because they don't want to cater to the games that a lot of people want to play with them. Because they've paid the dues. And I know it's a problem because when people are dealing with business, sometimes they don't want the intervention of people who want to stand them up and make them treat them right. Because they have an idea of how to use the music. And hopefully I'll be able to make a difference in the way the Music Commission will start embracing the music. And the idea of the workshop was to create a setting where guys who desired to play modern jazz could play without someone standing over them and trying to dictate where the music would evolve. Because we don't know where the music would evolve if it was not suppressed and controlled by a lot of times non-musical people. And a lot of times some of the answers to frustration and all that comes from the kind of music that we listen to. And you may be depressed and go on and put on a particular record that will just cool you out. And I think radio stations, especially in New Orleans, should take a stronger responsibility as to what kind of music is played. So you know appreciation for a lot of the public broadcast stations, they seem to have a greater sensitivity to playing broader forms of music. And I think that's needed. And when you can develop a different kind of closeness with people who have control over what's marketed, I think a lot of things in this city will change.
